name: Compton Dundon Yew

location.address: St Andrew's Church, Compton Dundon, Somerset

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, tree ID 376 (Tim Hills 1997)

access: Free. Open public churchyard, yew inside a low wall SSE of the church.
transport: Village near Street, Somerset; bus services from Street and Somerton run through Compton Dundon (check current timetable). No railway.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the big hollow trunk standing inside a low wall. It is south-south-east of St Andrew's church, in the churchyard.
verify_notes: Girth 742cm at 30cm (Hills 1997). Ground-level girth 24ft 9in (Hills 2000), 23ft 9in (Norton 2014). Hollow; Edmund Rack (d. 1787) surveyed the churchyard and called it 'a very old yew with a fine top; the body is hollow and measures 23ft in circumference'. Rev. R. Kelland recorded in 1954 that locally it was credited with about 1,000 years. Wikipedia assesses it over 1700 years (unsourced popular figure). Male tree. Alive: remeasured 2014. Pin: AYG grid ref ST47953252 converted to WGS84, approximate (church-yard level). Age: AYG girth class, not a dating; AYG counts 7 to 9 m girths as probably over 800 years; Wikipedia's 'over 1700 years' and the 1954 rector's 'about 1,000 years' are popular claims, not dated.
story:
Edmund Rack measured this yew in the 1780s, and in the 230 years since, on paper, it has barely changed. Rack, who surveyed the churchyard before his death in 1787, called it a very old yew with a fine top, and noted that the body was hollow and 23 feet round. Tim Hills found 24 feet 9 at ground level in 2000. Peter Norton measured 23 feet 9 in 2014. Different heights, different tapes, and still the same tree within a foot or two.

That stillness is why nobody can tell you its age from its waist. The Ancient Yew Group's figure is 742 centimetres at 30 centimetres off the ground, and yews of this size fall in its class of probably over 800 years, an estimate from girth and not a dating. Locally it was credited with about 1,000 years, the rector Rev. R. Kelland recorded in 1954. Wikipedia goes further, over 1,700, with nothing behind the number. We give you all three and the honest answer, which is that it is very old and undated.

It is a male tree, still hollow, standing inside a low wall to the south-south-east of St Andrew's. Rack would recognise it.

name: Ashbrittle Yew
age_estimate: over 1,000 years, popular claims far older

location.address: St John the Baptist Church, Ashbrittle, Somerset

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, tree ID 255 (Tim Hills 1997)

access: Free. Open public churchyard on a hilltop.
transport: Remote hilltop village west of Wellington, Somerset; no railway, no regular bus found (check). Drive.

location_site.name: St John the Baptist Church churchyard

how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the grassy mound it grows on, about 15 metres across, with a few headstones round its edge. It stands south-east of the church of St John the Baptist.
verify_notes: Girth 1217cm at 5cm (AYG tree 255, photos 1848, 1997, 2014). Grows on a tumulus (about 1.5m high, 15m across) SE of the church, thought possibly Bronze Age but unproven. One of the 50 Great British Trees chosen 2002 for the Golden Jubilee. Folklore: childless couples at its base conceive within a year. Wikipedia says believed over 3,000 years; Church Times 2015 reports it under the weather (condition check, still standing 2015). Mound edges hold a few headstones. Pin: AYG grid ref ST05202134 converted to WGS84, approximate (church-yard level). Age: AYG girth class, not a dating; girth 1217cm at 5cm on a mound; popular claims of 3,000 to 4,000 years are undated and not repeated here as fact. Writing pass 2026-11-04: lead photo Geograph 119778 (Martin Bodman, 'Ashbrittle: the Ashbrittle Yew', 2006) approved; Geograph 6909907 (Rob Purvis, 2021) also shows it standing in 2021.
story:
The Ashbrittle yew grows on top of a mound that may be a Bronze Age burial barrow. Nobody has proved it. The mound is about one and a half metres high and fifteen across, it sits south-east of the church of St John the Baptist on its hilltop, and a few headstones stand round its edge. Whatever is underneath, the yew has claimed it.

Its girth is enormous. The Ancient Yew Group recorded 12.17 metres at five centimetres off the ground,. For that size the Group's banding suggests well over 1,000 years. Wikipedia repeats a belief that it is over 3,000, and you will meet bolder figures still. None of them is a dating, and we do not repeat them as fact.

In 2002 the Tree Council chose it as one of 50 Great British Trees for the Queen's Golden Jubilee. Local folklore gives it another reputation. It says a childless couple who visit its base will conceive within a year. In 2015 the Church Times reported it looking under the weather, and it was still standing then.

It is a long way out, a hilltop village west of Wellington with no regular bus, and the drive is the price of standing next to it.

name: Kingston St Mary Yew

location.address: Church of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Kingston St Mary, Somerset

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, tree ID 544 (Tim Hills 2001)

access: Free. Open public churchyard, yew SW of the church.
transport: Village north of Taunton; local bus to Kingston St Mary from Taunton (check timetable). No railway.

location_site.name: Church of the Blessed Virgin Mary churchyard

how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the ring of separate trunks, fragments of one hollow yew that split apart. It stands south-west of the Church of the Blessed Virgin Mary.
verify_notes: Ground girth 1003cm (Hills 2001); Wondermondo gives 10.03m. Ancient trunk long since divided by a hollow into four fragments (Hills 2001) that stand as separate trunks, ivy-filled in 2001. Photo update 2016. AYG found no early reference to this yew. Church c1225. Pin: AYG grid ref ST22272971 converted to WGS84, approximate (church-yard level). Age: AYG girth class, not a dating; ground girth 1003cm (split into fragments, so girth is of the whole ring); AYG class Ancient 7m+.
story:
This yew broke into four pieces long ago and carried on as four trees. When Tim Hills recorded it in 2001, the ancient trunk had been split by its own hollow into separate fragments, standing apart in a ring and filled with ivy. Measured round the outside of that ring at ground level, the tree came to 10.03 metres, a figure Wondermondo repeats.

That number describes the whole circle, not a single stem, so treat it as the footprint of the old tree rather than the width of any one trunk. Yews this size fall in the Ancient Yew Group's top class, seven metres and up, which puts it in the band they call ancient. There is no dating behind it, and nobody has found an early written reference to this yew at all. For a tree of this size in a church that dates from about 1225, that silence is its own small mystery.

What survives is a ring of trunks south-west of the Church of the Blessed Virgin Mary, in a village just north of Taunton. Photographs were updated in 2016. If you know anything older about it, a mention in a parish history or a sketch, tell us. Somebody in eight centuries of this churchyard must have noticed it.

name: Broadwindsor Yew

location.address: St John the Baptist Church, Broadwindsor, Dorset

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, tree ID 301 (Tim Hills 1998)

access: Free. Open public churchyard; yew on a prominent mound E of the church.
transport: Village between Beaminster and Crewkerne, Dorset; infrequent bus (check). Drive.

location_site.name: St John the Baptist Church churchyard

how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the cluster of about 15 stems rising together from a raised mound. It stands east of the church of St John the Baptist.
verify_notes: Girth 1034cm at ground (AYG tree 301); stems on mound counted: about 15 trunks in 1998, trunk circumferences 0.9 to 1.8m (Wondermondo), mound about 1.2m (Wondermondo) or 4ft (2015). Possibly cut back to a stump at the 1867/68 restoration (AYG asks the question, a photo of 1867 shows a stump-like tree). Below average health 2015, photographed 2024. Male. Church c1180. Pin: AYG grid ref ST4377702650 converted to WGS84, approximate (church-yard level). Age: AYG girth class, not a dating; AYG class Ancient 7m+, girth 1034cm at ground (a 1994 book gave 33ft); but this is a multi-stem mass on a mound, so girth overstates one trunk.
story:
Victorian restorers may have cut this yew down to a stump, and it answered with fifteen trunks. A photograph from 1867, the time of the church's restoration, shows something that looks like a stump where the tree stands, and the Ancient Yew Group asks the obvious question without being able to settle it. What grew back is certainly not a single trunk. In 1998 the Group counted about 15 stems rising from a raised mound east of the church, each between 0.9 and 1.8 metres round, by Wondermondo's figures.

Measured around the whole mass at ground level, it comes to 10.34 metres. That reads as a giant, but it is a girth of many stems together, so it overstates any one of them. The Group puts yews of this size in its top class, ancient at seven metres and over, and that is an estimate from size, not a date.

It is a male tree, and it has had a hard time lately. Its health was recorded as below average in 2015, and it was photographed again in 2024. The church of St John the Baptist dates from about 1180, and the mound the yew grows on stands about 1.2 metres high.

If the stump story is true, this is what a yew does when you take it to the ground. It comes back, many times over.

name: Woolland Yew

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, tree ID 859 (Tim Hills 1998)

access: Free. Open public churchyard; yew S of the church.
transport: Hamlet in the Blackmore Vale, Dorset, between Blandford Forum and Sturminster Newton; no practical public transport found. Drive.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the sheer bulk of the trunk, over nine metres round near the ground. It stands south of the small 1855 church in Woolland churchyard.
verify_notes: Girth 947cm at 30cm (Norton 2012); matches 1944 figure of 31ft 4in published in Vaughan Cornish, The Churchyard Yew and Immortality (so little change in 70 years). Photographed 2026 (Peter Norton). Church built 1855 on an early Saxon site. Baxter, The Eternal Yew (quoted by AYG, unverified) calls it possibly the only yew to have sheltered three or four churches. Flagged: one source family (AYG plus its quoted books). Pin: AYG grid ref ST7761806972 converted to WGS84, approximate (church-yard level). Age: AYG girth class, not a dating; AYG class Ancient 7m+; girths 31ft 4in (1944, Gardner for Cornish) and 31ft at 1ft (1998), 947cm at 30cm (2012 Norton, 31ft 1in). Writing pass 2026-11-04: lead photo Geograph 4532427 (Maurice D Budden, 'Ancient yew tree in Woolland churchyard', 2015) approved.
story:
The church beside this yew was built in 1855, and the yew may have watched three or four churches come and go before it. That is the suggestion of Baxter's book The Eternal Yew, quoted by the Ancient Yew Group, which calls it possibly the only yew to have sheltered so many. It is one writer's claim, not a record. The ground it rests on is real enough. The present church stands on an early Saxon site in the Blackmore Vale.

The tree itself is a great stout yew south of that church, and it barely changes. In 1944 it was measured for Vaughan Cornish's The Churchyard Yew and Immortality at 31 feet 4 inches. In 1998 it was 31 feet at one foot up. In 2012 Peter Norton found 947 centimetres at 30 centimetres, which is 31 feet 1. Seventy years, three tapes and almost no movement, which tells you a great deal about how slowly an old yew lives.

The Ancient Yew Group puts yews of this girth in its top class, seven metres and over, an estimate from size rather than a dating. It was photographed again in 2026. Woolland is a hamlet with no practical bus, so plan to drive, and give the tree more time than the church.

name: Wimborne St Giles Yew

location.address: St Giles Church, Wimborne St Giles, Dorset

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, tree ID 2183 (Peter Andrews 2006)

access: Free. Open public churchyard beside the entrance to St Giles Park.
transport: Village north of Wimborne Minster, Dorset; Wilts and Dorset bus in the area (check). Drive.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk splitting into six big limbs round a central branch at about eight feet. It stands east-south-east of St Giles church; the slim columnar yew to the south-east is a younger one.
verify_notes: Girth 721cm at 120cm (Andrews 2006), male, branching at about 8ft with six large limbs round a huge central branch; photographed 2026 (Norton). Earliest mention 1884, The Quiver (Lord Shaftesbury pointed it out). A second, columnar male yew (343cm at 2ft) grows SE. Church rebuilt 18th century. Flagged: AYG only. Pin: AYG grid ref SU0319111952 converted to WGS84, approximate (church-yard level). Age: AYG girth class, not a dating; AYG class Ancient 7m+, girth 721cm at 120cm. Writing pass 2026-11-04: Geograph 2787867 ('Yew tree, St Giles Church') held: a massive trunk, very likely the old yew rather than the slim columnar one, but neither title nor geotag says which of the two yews.
story:
This yew first appeared in print in 1884, because Lord Shaftesbury pointed it out. The magazine was The Quiver, and the churchyard sits beside the entrance to St Giles Park. More than 140 years later it is still the tree to look at in this village north of Wimborne Minster.

Its shape is what sets it apart. At about eight feet up the trunk divides into six large limbs arranged round a huge central branch. Peter Andrews measured the girth at 721 centimetres at 120 centimetres up in 2006, taken near chest height, where most churchyard yew records are taken much lower.

It is a male tree. The Ancient Yew Group puts a yew of this girth in its ancient class, seven metres and over, as an estimate from size. The church beside it was rebuilt in the 18th century. The yew was photographed again in 2026.

Do not confuse it with its neighbour. A second male yew grows to the south-east, slim and columnar and about 3.4 metres round. The one you want is the broad one east-south-east of the church.

name: Lytchett Matravers Yew

location.address: St Mary the Virgin Church, Lytchett Matravers, Dorset

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, tree ID 579 (Tim Hills 1999)

access: Free. Open public churchyard, yew by the north door side.
transport: Village northwest of Poole; local bus from Poole (check). Drive easier.

location_site.name: St Mary the Virgin Church churchyard

how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the larger of two yews by the north door, about 6.5 metres round against the younger yew's 3.6. It stands north-west of St Mary the Virgin church.
verify_notes: Girth 648cm at 30cm (AYG tree 579); earlier 21ft 3in and 21ft 10in just above 5ft (Hills 1999). First noted in the 1855 Post Office Directory. A younger yew (11ft 10in girth in 2011) grows nearby, do not confuse. Church c1200, Grade I. Pin: AYG grid ref SY9359196171 converted to WGS84, approximate (church-yard level). Age: AYG girth class, not a dating; AYG class Ancient 5m-7m (probably 600+); blog claims of 1600 years or AD 590 (National Churches Trust) are undated popular claims, not used.
story:
The first written record of this yew is in a Post Office Directory of 1855, a book printed to help people find tradesmen and addresses. It is a modest debut for a tree the Ancient Yew Group now classes as ancient.

The measurements are steady. Tim Hills recorded 21 feet 3 and 21 feet 10 just above five feet in 1999, and the Group's current figure is 648 centimetres at 30 centimetres. Yews between five and seven metres fall in its band of probably more than 600 years. That is an estimate from girth, and you will find much bolder claims online, 1,600 years or a planting in AD 590. Nobody has dated it, and we do not repeat those as fact.

The church of St Mary the Virgin is Grade I and dates from about 1200, so even the cautious estimate puts the tree in the same company as the building. It grows on the north-west side of the church, close to the north door.

Bring your eye for a second yew. A much younger tree grows nearby, 11 feet 10 inches round in 2011, which would be impressive anywhere else and is easily mistaken for the old one. The ancient yew is the larger, by about ten feet of girth.

name: Dinder Yew

location.address: St Michael and All Angels Church, Dinder, Somerset

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, tree ID 407 (Tim Hills 1997)

access: Free. Open public churchyard; yew SE of the church.
transport: Village 4km east of Wells; bus from Wells (check). No railway.

location_site.name: St Michael and All Angels Church churchyard

how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the big yew, over nine metres round at the ground. It stands south-east of St Michael and All Angels church in Dinder.
verify_notes: Girth 912cm at ground (Hills 1997; photo Norton 2015). 1857 Guide to Minehead and Its Environs (quoted by AYG; AYG gives the identical sentence for Dunster, so treat as unreliable) described 'a yew of great age and formerly of considerable extent'. Church possibly Saxon site, Grade II*. Flagged: AYG register plus church Wikipedia page, which does not itself describe the yew. Pin: AYG grid ref ST57524459 converted to WGS84, approximate (church-yard level). Age: AYG girth class, not a dating; AYG class Ancient 7m+, girth 912cm at ground.
story:
The only old description of the Dinder yew may belong to another tree. An 1857 Guide to Minehead and Its Environs, quoted by the Ancient Yew Group, describes a yew of great age and formerly of considerable extent. The trouble is that the Group gives the identical sentence for the yew at Dunster, so it probably cannot be trusted for either. Dinder's tree is left with its measurements and not much else.

The measurements are worth having. Tim Hills found 912 centimetres at ground level in 1997, which puts it in the Group's top class of yews over seven metres, ancient by their banding. That is an estimate from girth and not a date. Peter Norton photographed it in 2015.

It stands south-east of St Michael and All Angels, a Grade II* church that may stand on a Saxon site. The village is about four kilometres east of Wells, which makes this an easy add-on to a day in the cathedral city.

If you know of a better old record, something that names Dinder and not Dunster, tell us. This yew deserves a first mention of its own.

name: Combe Florey Yew

location.address: St Peter and St Paul Church, Combe Florey, Somerset

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, tree ID 375 (Tim Hills 1997)

access: Free. Open public churchyard, yew S of the church on the east side.
transport: Village NW of Taunton; Taunton to Williton bus along the A358 passes (check). No railway.

location_site.name: St Peter and St Paul Church churchyard

how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the larger of the two yews, over eight metres round near the ground. It stands south of the church on the east side; the young yew grows north-west.
verify_notes: Girth 813cm at 5cm (AYG tree 375, photo 2015). Two female yews in the churchyard: the ancient one S of the church and a young tree NW. Church c1300, Grade I. Flagged: AYG only for the yew. Pin: AYG grid ref ST15053117 converted to WGS84, approximate (church-yard level). Age: AYG girth class, not a dating; AYG class Ancient 7m+, girth 813cm at 5cm.
story:
Combe Florey's churchyard holds two female yews, and centuries separate them. The young one grows north-west of the church of St Peter and St Paul. The old one stands south of it, on the east side, and it is the reason to come.

The Ancient Yew Group measured it at 813 centimetres, taken five centimetres off the ground, where a yew's trunk flares widest. That puts it in their top class of seven metres and over, which they treat as ancient. It is an estimate from size, not a dating, and nobody has put a year on it.

The church beside it dates from about 1300 and is Grade I. On the size estimate the yew is older still, but that is the estimate talking.

Female yews are the ones that bear the red, fleshy cups around their seeds in autumn; males only shed pollen. Here you can see the same kind of tree at two ends of its life, a short walk apart, and judge for yourself how many centuries the difference represents. Nobody has written that number down, and if you know it, tell us.

name: Chilcompton Yew

location.address: St John the Baptist Church, Chilcompton, Somerset

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, tree ID 353 (Tim Hills 1997)

access: Free. Open public churchyard; yew SW of the church.
transport: Village near Midsomer Norton, Somerset; bus from Midsomer Norton and Bath (check).

location_site.name: St John the Baptist Church churchyard

how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the big yew south-west of the church of St John the Baptist, about 7.8 metres round at its base.
verify_notes: Girth 780cm at root crown (AYG tree 353, photo Hills 2006). Also on the Bath and Wells diocese list of ancient yews (2013: 1 ancient). Flagged: AYG only, last photo 2006, no recent life check. Pin: AYG grid ref ST64695240 converted to WGS84, approximate (church-yard level). Age: AYG girth class, not a dating; AYG class Ancient 7m+, girth 780cm at root crown.
story:
When the Diocese of Bath and Wells listed its ancient yews in 2013, Chilcompton had exactly one, and this is it. It stands south-west of the church of St John the Baptist, on the northern edge of a village near Midsomer Norton.

Tim Hills measured it at 780 centimetres at the root crown, where the trunk meets the roots. That is big enough for the Ancient Yew Group's top class, seven metres and over, the band they call ancient. As with any age read from a tape, it is an estimate from size and not a dating.

We should be plain about one thing. The most recent photograph we know of dates from 2006, and we have found no later record. We cannot promise you what you will find. If you visit, a photograph would settle it for everyone who comes after you.

Buses run to the village from Midsomer Norton and Bath, so this is an ancient yew you can reach without a car, which in rural Somerset is not a given.
